cards.front: Which six elements make up most living matter?
cards.back: **Carbon**, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur (C, H, O, N, P, S). They matter because of the combinations they form, not as separate ingredients.
cards.hint: Think about which elements appear in water and proteins.

cards.front: Why can carbon build such a wide variety of molecules?
cards.back: Carbon forms four **covalent bonds**, so its atoms can link into chains, branches, and rings. Double bonds change the shape and behavior of the framework.
cards.hint: Focus on how many bonds each carbon atom can form.

cards.front: How do the kinds, numbers, and arrangement of atoms affect a molecule?
cards.back: They determine the molecule's **properties**. The arrangement of atoms affects its properties as well as its composition.
cards.hint: Consider what changes when atoms are added or rearranged.

cards.back: A substance made of only one kind of **atom**.
A chemical bond in which **atoms share electrons**.
A group of atoms held together by **chemical bonds**.

cards.front: How many hydrogen and oxygen atoms does one water molecule contain?
cards.back: **Two** hydrogen atoms and **one** oxygen atom, as shown by $\mathrm{H_2O}$.
cards.hint: Read the subscripts in the formula.

cards.front: Where does phosphorus appear in cellular molecules?
cards.back: In **nucleic acids** and phospholipids, and in phosphate groups bonded to oxygen atoms.
cards.hint: Think about the building blocks of DNA and cell membranes.

cards.back: A group containing a **phosphorus** atom bonded to oxygen atoms, which can attach to another part of a molecule.

cards.front: Where does sulfur occur in cells?
cards.back: In some **amino acids**, which are the building blocks of proteins.
An element needed in a very **small amount**. The small amount required does not show how important the element is.

cards.front: What role does iron play in many animals?
cards.back: Iron is part of **hemoglobin**, which carries oxygen in the blood.
cards.hint: Think about how oxygen travels around the body.

cards.front: Does needing only a small amount of an element mean it is optional?
cards.back: No. Too little of an **essential element** can disrupt cell function, even though cells need only a small amount.
cards.hint: Consider what happens when a needed element is missing.

cards.front: Are the six main elements the only ones cells need?
cards.back: No. Other elements, such as iron and magnesium, are **essential** in smaller amounts.
